Photograph: Tetiana Dzhafarova/AFP/Getty Images View image in fullscreen Ukrainian firefighters at a site hit by Russian ballistic missiles, Kyiv, 5 August 2026. Photograph: Tetiana Dzhafarova/AFP/Getty Images Opinion Ukraine Patriot missiles have been a godsend for Ukraine against Putin, but they’re running out. Kyiv needs help and fast Jack Watling Europe and Nato have known for years that interceptor production can’t keep up with demand and now disaster looms, putting us all in danger Fri 14 Aug 2026 04.54 EDT Last modified on Fri 14 Aug 2026 05.55 EDT Share “I nvincible.” That was how Vladimir Putin described Russia’s latest generation of ballistic missiles in 2018 . In 2022 he would unleash this arsenal to strike across Ukraine, hitting command centres, critical infrastructure and airfields. Then, in 2023, Ukraine received Patriot air defence systems from its international partners. The US-supplied missile interceptor would prove to be an effective shield against Russian strikes. But this year, supplies of Patriot missiles have run out and Kyiv has suffered the consequences. Intercepts have gone from more than 70% to none, so that night after night Russia strikes Ukraine’s infrastructure with impunity. This tragedy was long foretold, and there are no quick fixes. While the military narrative of the war has largely been of cheap mass-produced Ukrainian weapons overwhelming exquisite Russian military hardware, most of the serious damage from Russia’s long-range strikes has come from cruise and ballistic missiles, and Ukraine’s campaign has suffered for want of them. Countering ballistic missiles is not a simple or cheap activity . To intercept a tactical ballistic missile, such as Russia’s Iskander, a defensive system needs to be remarkably sophisticated. Its target will be descending from the high atmosphere at more than five times the speed of sound. The incoming missile will also be manoeuvring through the air, rather than following a predictable ballistic trajectory. The defensive system needs to be able to track the precise location of this incoming missile and communicate this to the intercepting missile, allowing the latter to adjust course while climbing against gravity. Building the radars, data links and interceptors for such a task involves a huge amount of research and development, and across Nato most states have been happy for Washington to invest over decades to make the Patriot up to the job. The US and licensed manufacturers in Germany and Japan are able to produce about 840 Patriot interceptors a year. About 240 of these are older, larger PAC-2 interceptors, which climb until they are close to the target and then explode – meaning they must carry the weight of a warhead to the target – and 600 are PAC-3s, which are smaller and fly directly into the target. The latter approach is more effective but requires even more precise navigation. The former can be used against other target types. Russia produces about 750 Iskander missiles a year and is looking to increase production. In addition, Russia uses air-launched Kinzhal ballistic missiles and repurposed air-defence missiles to conduct strikes, along with its arsenal of cruise missiles and drones. To have a high probability of success, it is generally recommended to fire two to three interceptors against each ballistic missile. When you also factor in that the launchers themselves can only protect a relatively small area, and Ukraine is a vast country, then it becomes clear that Kyiv would ideally have three to four times the annual global production capacity of Patriot missiles to protect itself. Countries supporting Ukraine have therefore had to give their own stockpiles to Kyiv. Even before the US decision to attack Iran, western allies were nervous about depleting their own stocks by giving Patriot missiles to Ukraine, knowing that it would take a long time for them to be resupplied. The US attack on Iran – prompting Tehran to fire ballistic missiles across the Middle East – has created an acute global shortage. Where Russia usually fires fewer than 10 ballistic missiles in a single attack, Iran has launched upwards of 170 a day during the current and last year’s war. A portion of Iran’s missiles were also advanced. In one instance, it took 17 Patriot interceptors to defeat a missile. And Iran has many more missiles in storage. skip past newsletter promotion Free newsletter | Weekly Sign up to Matters of Opinion Guardian columnists and writers on what they’ve been debating, thinking about, reading, and more after newsletter promotion Amid war in Ukraine, the fleeting moments of despair and salvation I witness are what truly tell the story | Charlotte Higgins Read more The point is that Ukraine is not going to receive enough Patriots between now and the winter to save its critical national infrastructure, irrespective of whether some countries make the political gesture of releasing a few more from their stockpiles. At this point, Kyiv must plan for a winter with severely disrupted power, and disperse and fortify life-support systems such as water, sanitation, power and heating. Kyiv is trying to convince the US to activate Starlink satellite navigation modules over Russian territory to enable its drones to hunt for the Russian missile launchers. But, as the US recently found in Iran, pulling off this kind of mission over a large area is extremely difficult. Another line of effort in Kyiv is to attack the production of Russia’s ballistic missiles. These factories are well defended. To succeed, Ukraine’s partners will need to expand the funding and industrial capacity behind Ukraine’s nascent cruise-missile industry, or reopen questions of providing weapons systems such as Germany’s Taurus (which Berlin didn’t provide to Ukraine for fear of military escalation). But the real lesson here is that Nato members have abjectly failed in defence planning. The numbers in this equation have been known since before 2022 and yet the investments to expand Patriot production (or mature alternative systems such as the Franco-Italian SAMP-T ) have not been made. Such a level of complacency is devastating for Ukraine today, but it also risks Europe being bereft of defences in the future. It remains remarkable that Europe – watching the consequences unfold on its very borders – has remained so idle. https://www.politico.eu/article/russia-h.text: U.S. President Donald Trump said Russia's energy sector had been badly affected by the war in Ukraine and called for an end to the "ridiculous" and "never ending" conflict between Moscow and Kyiv. In a post on Truth Social Monday, Trump said, "Russia has unfortunately lost control of its Diesel Oil Industry due to its War with Ukraine." He referred to the intensification in Ukrainian attacks on Russia's energy infrastructure, which have disabled almost half of its refining capacity. "A large number of their Diesel refineries have been blown up and are, at least temporarily, out of commission," he wrote. Advertisement Advertisement Trump ended his post with a demand to end the conflict in Ukraine. "This ridiculous and never-ending war with Ukraine must be ended," he said. "The whole World suffers as 25,000 people, mostly soldiers, are being killed each month. What a shame!" Responding to Trump's message, Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said on X that his country was ready to stop its attacks on Russia if the Kremlin did the same for Ukraine. "Ukraine’s energy sector, critical infrastructure, and our food exports must stop being targets for Russia, and this will lead to matching de-escalation steps on our part," he wrote, adding, "the nature of war is now such that the aggressor will suffer as well." Earlier this month , Trump called on Ukraine to stop targeting Russia's energy infrastructure, saying attacks on the diesel industry were "hurting the world" by causing fuel shortages. The two men are set to meet in New York Tuesday — a meeting Zelenskyy said "could change a lot," noting that there was "diplomatic momentum" in current talks. "There are ideas for de-escalation steps and for addressing fundamental security issues – energy security, food security, and the protection of human life," said the Ukrainian president . "We are working together with the American team and are ready to take really serious steps." Advertisement Advertisement

https://www.dw.com/en/hundreds-of-french.text: Skip to content Skip to main menu Skip to more DW sites https://p.dw.com/p/5Nkg4 The school protests have spread nationwide, as here in Lyon Image: Laurent Cipriani/AP Photo/picture alliance Advertisement Several hundred schools in France closed totally or partially on Monday amid security fears following a wave of nationwide student protests, the education minister has said. The protests by pupils complaining of poor conditions began at one Paris school on September 17 but last week mutated into sometimes violent demonstrations across the nation. A 15-year-old boy in the northern town of Lens sustained a severe injury to his hand amid one of the protests on Monday. French news agency AFP cited a police union source as saying he appeared to have picked up a sting ball grenade, another term for a type of tear gas grenade also often called a blast ball, and it exploded in his hand. The demonstrations have started to dominate France's political debate just a few months before presidential elections that will choose a successor to Emmanuel Macron, who is approaching term limit. France students protest school conditions To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video Why are the schools staying closed? Education Minister Edouard Geffray said on Sunday that lessons would be totally or partly suspended in some 400 to 500 high schools on Monday, as the security conditions "have not been fulfilled." According to Geffray, the schools were being closed mainly as a precaution, with more large protests planned for Tuesday. Geffray said the number of schools remaining closed on Monday would be similar to that on Friday but that there was planned to be a "partial, progressive return to lessons." He said 24 schools had been "burned or ransacked" and 78 education staff members injured since the protests began. "There are activists — particularly from the far left — who have infiltrated the high school student movement, hijacked it from the students themselves, and engaged in extreme violence," Geffray said. "Clearly, this poses a risk to both our staff and our students," he added. Several schools have been damaged amid the protests Image: CLPRESS/ABACA/picture alliance Valerie Pecresse, the president of the Ile-de-France region surrounding the capital, said that more than a third of the 468 schools in the region would be shut on Monday. What are the school protesters saying? The protesting teenagers at French upper high schools, called Lycees , have complained of high rates of absenteeism by teachers, school days that are too long and dilapidated facilities. They have also protested at the lack of adequate cooling on hot summer days, with some towns seeing temperatures of 40 degrees Celsius (104 Fahrenheit) last summer in a country without widespread air conditioning. Organizers have called for the protests to continue on Tuesday, saying the government was still failing to propose "concrete measures" to remedy the situation. On Sunday, Prime Minister Sebastien Lecornu urged local authorities to make it a priority to fill gaps left by long-term absences and unfilled posts. He also called a meeting for Tuesday with regional presidents to discuss renovating school buildings that are often in poor condition. Violent incidents at the school protests The protests have been marked by several violent incidents, with security forces sometimes using tear gas and batons to disperse the young protesters. More than 5,000 people, 85% of them minors, have been arrested since the start of the movement. On Sunday, a 16-year-old was detained after a 59-year-old teacher was hit and doused with gasoline on the sidelines of a protest in the southern town of La Ciotat. Last week, a group of young people was filmed beating and kicking a policeman on the ground in the eastern town of Belfort. The French branch of rights group Amnesty International last week described the action taken by police as "disproportionate." Interior Minister Laurent Nunez has, however, defended security forces, saying they were "not cracking down on young people" but rather "protecting" school and university students wishing to "peacefully voice their demands." https://pakobserver.net/cheapest-countri.text: Cheapest Countries for a Master’s Degree for Pakistani Students — 2026 Update By Web Desk Lahore | Sep 28, 2026 | Updated 2 weeks ago Follow us If you are looking for affordable Master’s degree abroad, Pakistan Observer brings a guide to several countries offering relatively low tuition fees, manageable living costs and fully funded scholarship opportunities in 2026–27. For Pakistani students planning to study in EU, US and other nations, the biggest challenge is often not finding university but understanding the total cost, scholarship opportunities, admission requirements and financial commitments involved. This guide covers fully funded scholarships, affordable study destinations, tuition estimates, living costs and important checks students should make before applying. For Pakistani students, studying abroad generally falls into two broad categories. Fully funded scholarships in which tuition and major living expenses are covered and then there is Self-funded study in which students pay tuition, living expenses and other costs themselves. Scholarships Fully funded scholarships are important for Pakistani students because they can cover most of the major expenses associated with studying abroad. Scholarship Region Coverage Deadline Stipendium Hungaricum Hungary Tuition, monthly stipend, accommodation contribution, insurance Usually Jan–Feb Türkiye Bursları Türkiye Tuition, stipend, housing, insurance, flight, Turkish language course 10 Jan–20 Feb 2027 Chinese Government Scholarship (CSC) China Tuition, housing, stipend HEC-nominated round historically early January DAAD Germany Monthly stipend and support 15 Oct 2026 for the main round cited Erasmus Mundus Multiple EU countries Fully funded joint master’s Many around mid-January Chevening UK Full funding Early November 2026 Fulbright / USEFP USA Full master’s/PhD funding Around May What Pakistani Students Should Do Do not wait until the deadline month to start preparing. 6–12 months before the deadline Decide your field of study. Prepare your CV. Collect transcripts and degree documents. Identify suitable universities and programs. Arrange recommendation letters. Prepare your statement of purpose or motivation letter. Check IELTS, MOI and other English-language requirements. Review HEC requirements where applicable. 1–3 months before the deadline Finalize university choices. Complete scholarship applications. Obtain any missing documents. Check passport validity. Submit applications well before the deadline. Germany Germany is one of the most important destinations for Pakistani students because many public universities do not charge tuition fees to non-EU students, although students still have to pay semester contributions and cover their living expenses. Tuition Fee Category Approx. Cost per Year Approx. PKR Most German states €0 tuition + €200–800 semester contributions PKR 63,000–254,000 Baden-Württemberg €3,000 PKR 951,000 TUM master’s €8,000–12,000 PKR 2.5–3.8 million Universities mentioned for Germany include LMU Munich, Bonn, Cologne, Münster, TU Berlin, TU Dresden, Leipzig and RWTH Aachen. In Baden-Württemberg, examples include Heidelberg, KIT, Stuttgart and Freiburg. TUM is listed separately because of its higher master’s tuition. Living Costs A rough example for a year in Leipzig or Dresden comes to around €9,300, including fees. It is important to remember that “tuition-free” does not mean “cost-free.” Students still need money for: Accommodation Food Transportation Health insurance Semester contributions Visa-related expenses Financial proof A German blocked account of roughly €11,900 per year is mentioned as a financial requirement, although the amount can change. Academic Opportunities Germany is particularly relevant for students interested in: Computer Science Artificial Intelligence Engineering Data Science Physics Business and Economics Environmental Science Agriculture Germany also has more than 1,900 English-taught master’s programs. Hungary Hungary offers both self-funded and scholarship-based study opportunities. Self-Funded Study Approximate tuition: €2,000–3,000 per year That is roughly PKR 634,000–951,000 per year using the exchange-rate assumptions above. Universities mentioned include: Budapest University of Technology and Economics (BME) ELTE Corvinus University University of Debrecen University of Szeged Scholarship Route The Stipendium Hungaricum scholarship can provide: Tuition coverage Monthly stipend Accommodation contribution Insurance For Pakistani applicants, applications go through HEC. This makes Hungary relevant both for students looking for relatively affordable self-funded study and those seeking scholarship support. Poland Poland is presented as one of the lower-cost European destinations. Tuition Approximate tuition: €1,500–4,000 per year That is around PKR 476,000–1.27 million per year. Universities mentioned include: Warsaw University of Technology AGH Kraków Wrocław University of Science and Technology Jagiellonian University Living Costs Estimated living expenses are around: €500–700 per month When comparing European destinations, students should look beyond tuition. A university with slightly higher tuition can still have a lower overall cost if accommodation and daily expenses are more affordable. Czech Republic The Czech Republic has two different tuition situations depending on the language of instruction. Czech-Taught Programs These can potentially be free. English-Taught Programs Approximate tuition: €1,000–4,000 per year That is roughly PKR 317,000–1.27 million per year. Universities mentioned include: Czech Technical University Charles University Brno University of Technology Masaryk University Estimated living expenses are approximately €500–750 per month. For Pakistani students seeking an English-taught master’s, it is important not to assume that the free-education rules for Czech-taught programs automatically apply. Austria The guide gives an approximate tuition figure of: €726.72 per semester or around: €1,450 per year ≈ PKR 461,000 for non-EU students. Universities mentioned include: TU Wien University of Vienna University of Graz University of Innsbruck The figures for Austria are older and approximate, so students should check the current tuition directly with the university before applying. France Approximate master’s tuition is listed at: €3,900 per year or around: PKR 1.24 million per year. However, some universities may waive the stated fee. Universities mentioned include: Paris-Saclay Sorbonne Lyon Grenoble Alpes Toulouse Students should check the exact university and program instead of assuming that every French university charges the same amount. Italy Italy has a different tuition structure because fees can depend on a student’s income. Approximate tuition: €500–4,000 per year or around: PKR 158,000–1.27 million per year. Universities mentioned include: Sapienza University of Rome University of Bologna University of Padua University of Naples Federico II Politecnico di Milano The Italian figures are rough and older estimates, so current fees should be confirmed directly with individual universities. Countries That Are No Longer Completely Free Students relying on older YouTube videos, blogs or social media posts should be particularly careful about claims that certain European countries offer completely free education to international students. The guide gives the following approximate figures: Denmark: €6,000–16,000 per year for non-EU students Finland: €4,000–18,000 per year Norway: Tuition fees for non-EU master’s students were introduced in 2023 Therefore, older claims that Norway is completely free for international students may no longer reflect the current situation. Pakistan to award 500 scholarships to Bangladeshi students United States The United States is substantially more expensive in this comparison, particularly for on-campus study. University/Program Approx. Tuition Approx Amount Georgia Tech Online $6,750–8,000 total for CS PKR 1.9–2.2 million University of the People $5,260–5,460 total PKR 1.5 million Fort Hays State Online $12,745 PKR 3.5 million Southeast Missouri State $14,976 PKR 4.2 million Missouri State $16,798 including insurance/fees PKR 4.7 million Minot State $17,604 PKR 4.9 million Cal State Long Beach $18,000 PKR 5.0 million UTEP $18,600 PKR 5.2 million FIU $19,000 PKR 5.3 million Wayne State $20,000 PKR 5.6 million Wyoming $19,500 PKR 5.4 million UT Dallas / San José State $20,000–30,000 PKR 5.6–8.3 million These figures are largely based on 2024–2026 guides and may have changed. Living Expenses Students should also budget around: $10,000–15,000 per year for living expenses. As a result, a two-year master’s degree can reach approximately: $35,000–60,000 or more depending on the university and lifestyle. Online vs On-Campus Study An online American degree can have a very different cost structure because students do not have the same on-campus living expenses. For example, an online Georgia Tech program can also avoid the need for a US student visa. However, students considering online degrees should check HEC recognition, particularly before enrolling in programs such as the University of the People. Türkiye For self-funded study, public-university tuition is estimated at around: $1,000–3,000 per year. Universities mentioned include: METU Istanbul Technical University Hacettepe University Ankara University Türkiye becomes particularly attractive from a financial perspective through the Türkiye Bursları scholarship. The scholarship can cover: Tuition Stipend Housing Insurance Flight Turkish language course The cited application window is 10 January to 20 February 2027. Malaysia Approximate tuition: $3,000–6,000 per year or around: PKR 834,000–1.67 million per year using the approximate exchange rate of $1 = PKR 278. Universities mentioned include: Universiti Malaya UKM UPM USM UTM Malaysia is presented as one of the more affordable options when tuition and living expenses are considered together. China Approximate tuition: $2,800–6,000 per year Public universities generally fall within this range, although elite institutions can charge more. The major scholarship route is the Chinese Government Scholarship (CSC). It can cover: Tuition Housing Stipend For Pakistani students, the HEC-nominated round has historically closed in early January. South Korea Approximate tuition: $3,000–6,000 per year Elite universities can charge more. The major scholarship mentioned is the Global Korea Scholarship (GKS). For students looking to reduce their financial burden through scholarships, South Korea is another destination worth exploring. What You Should Check Before Applying HEC Recognition Before paying an application fee or accepting an offer, check whether the university and degree meet the relevant HEC recognition requirements. This is especially important for: Online degrees Less familiar universities Foreign campuses Programs delivered through unusual arrangements A university being foreign or accredited in its home country does not automatically mean that every degree arrangement will meet Pakistani recognition requirements. English-Language Requirements Check whether your program requires: IELTS TOEFL or another English test MOI — Medium of Instruction Some universities may accept an MOI document, while others may still require a standardized English-language test. Proof of Funds Admission and scholarships are not the only financial considerations. For Germany, for example, the guide mentions a blocked account of roughly €11,900 per year, although the amount can change. Your financial planning should therefore account for: University costs + visa/financial-proof requirements + living expenses Student Application Checklist Before submitting an application, make sure A pénzt Ukrajnába vitt katonai felszerelések, fegyverek után térítik a tagállami kormányoknak. Korábban az Orbán-kormány hétszer engedett át ilyen egyhangú döntést az alapnál, amelyből az uniós tagállamoknak adnak részleges utótérítést EU-n kívüli országokba vitt hadisegély után. (Nem csak Ukrajnába, de más országoknál az előző magyar kormány sem blokkolta a kifizetéseket, sőt, 2024 februárjában kezdeményezte , hogy a csádi biztonság erősítésére is költsenek.) Az előző magyar kormány legalább egyszer konstruktívan tartózkodott 2023 márciusában . Ilyenkor jogilag kimarad, de elfogadja, hogy a határozat köti az EU-t. Még 2024 márciusában megkérdeztük a külügyi tárcát, hogy a másik hat esetben hogyan szavazott, és ha tartózkodott, élt-e a konstruktív tartózkodás lehetőségével. Az előző kormánytól soha nem kaptunk erre választ. „Magyarország nem szállít fegyvert ebbe a háborúba, nem is fogunk”, ezért nem visz lőszert, „ugyanakkor nem akadályozzuk meg, hogy a többiek azt csináljanak, amit akarnak” – magyarázta 2023 márciusában Szijjártó Péter volt külgazdasági és külügyminiszter. (Magyarországnak valóban nem kellett küldenie semmit, más tagállamoknak ment a pénz.) Szijjártó a blokkolásnál először arra hivatkozott, hogy az OTP-t háborús szponzorként listázták Ukrajnában, majd amikor az ukránok megszüntették a listát, más indokokra váltott. Közben 2024 márciusában egyhangúlag döntöttek, hogy további ötmilliárd euróval bővítik az alapot egy kifejezetten Ukrajnának szánt alzsebbel, a magyar kormány konstruktívan tartózkodott. A Politico júniusban arról írt, hogy a magyar kormány képviselője a külügyi döntéseket előkészítő Politikai és Biztonsági Bizottságban jelezte a kifizetés átengedését. A lap szerint ezzel 6,6 milliárd eurót adtak volna az uniós tagállamoknak, ekkora blokkolt összegről volt szó már 2024-ben is . A júniusi cikkről a megjelenésekor megkérdeztük a külügyi tárcát, de jelezték, hogy még nincs döntés. A mostani tanácsi közlemény nem 6,6, hanem 4,7 milliárd euróról szól, de a szöveg szerint még szeptemberben elkötelezték magukat, hogy jövőre további egymilliárd eurót engedélyeznek. Mellette az EU – még az előző magyar kormány alatt jóváhagyott – kiképzőmissziójára is adnak 230 millió eurót. A lap idézte Andrij Szibihát is, aki arról írt, hogy szerinte az alap segítségével Patriot légvédelmi rendszereket és ahhoz való elhárítórakétákat kellene venni, valamint „növelni a befektetéseket Ukrajna nagy hatótávolságú képességeibe”. Utóbbira az orosz vagyonból lefölözött hozamból költöttek, ami miatt Szijjártó pert kezdeményezett, de ez elbukott az EU bíróságán .
